beats.narration_text: Here's what a skill actually is: a folder Claude reads before it does the work. This one's called lbo-model, and inside it there's one file — SKILL.md — written in plain English, no hidden logic. Claude reads the file, then acts on what it says. The design choice worth naming: they put the routine on a page instead of baking it into the weights. Same file, same behavior, every run.

The pipeline lives in the file's Steps section. Claude reads each step and runs it in the order written — no branching, unless the file itself says branch. They optimized for guaranteed consistency at the expense of Claude's own judgment about the order. Same steps, every run.

Concretely, three moves. One — fill in the formulas the template already specifies. Two — validate the calculations against each other; if the sources and uses don't tie, flag it. Three — check the formatting against a professional standard. And because Claude reads your template's own structure before it touches a cell, the same three moves work on whatever LBO template you hand it — not one hard-coded layout. What the skill never does: pick the leverage, choose the exit multiple, or decide whether the deal makes sense. Those are inputs the template asks for, and the template asks a person.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Pick a template you already use — an LBO model, a DCF, a comps sheet, a budget, whatever — and ask the model to write you a SKILL.md for it: one folder, one file, three moves in order — fill in what the template specifies, validate the calculations against each other, check the formatting against a professional standard. Then have it read the file back and walk through exactly what it'll do before it touches anything. Go deeper: ask which fields in your template still need human judgment to fill — the numbers a checklist can't produce — and why they belong to a person, not a skill.

llm_exercise.prompt: I have a spreadsheet template I already use — for example [pick one: an LBO model, a DCF, a comps sheet, a monthly budget, a project scorecard]. Write me a SKILL.md — one file in a folder — that would let you fill it in reliably every time. Read the template's own structure first, then in order: fill each field with the specified formula or value, validate the whole thing against a set of consistency checks (name three that matter for this template), and check the formatting against a professional standard. Don't invent new fields; work with what's already there. Then read the file back to me and walk through exactly what you'll do — before you do it.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: ask which fields in the template can't be filled by a checklist — the ones that need judgment the file can't spell out — and explain why those belong to a person, not a skill.
